content: Adalimumab is a medication that can suppress your immune system, reducing your body’s ability to fight infections. This suppression can result in severe, potentially life-threatening infections, including fungal infections and bacterial infections such as tuberculosis. It is crucial to inform your doctor about your medical history, particularly if you have had any past, recent, or current infections. Additionally, let your doctor know if you have lived in or traveled to areas where certain fungal infections, such as coccidioidomycosis or histoplasmosis, are common, or if you have been in close contact with someone who has tuberculosis. These fungal infections are more prevalent in regions like the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys and the southwestern United States. Your doctor will test you for tuberculosis before and during treatment with this medication. Although rare, there is a risk of developing cancers, such as lymphoma or skin cancer, associated with this medication, particularly in children, teenagers, and young adults. This risk may also be related to your underlying medical condition. Discuss the potential risks and benefits of this treatment with your doctor. Adalimumab is used to alleviate pain and swelling caused by specific types of arthritis, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis. It is also prescribed for certain skin conditions, such as plaque psoriasis and hidradenitis suppurativa. The medication works by inhibiting a protein called tumor necrosis factor (TNF), which is part of the immune system and contributes to joint inflammation and damage in arthritis, as well as red, scaly patches in psoriasis. Adalimumab belongs to a class of drugs known as TNF blockers. Before starting adalimumab, read the Medication Guide and Instructions for Use provided by your pharmacist. Consult your healthcare provider for guidance on how to prepare and administer this medication. It is typically injected under the skin as directed by your doctor, usually every other week or, in some cases, once a week. The injection is administered in the thigh or abdomen. Dosage is determined based on your medical condition and response to treatment. For children, the dosage is also based on weight. If you are using this medication for conditions like psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa, Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis, or uveitis, your doctor may prescribe a different dosing schedule or a higher initial dose. Before injecting, allow the medication to reach room temperature by removing it from the refrigerator 15 to 30 minutes beforehand. Do not warm it using other methods, such as a microwave or hot water. Inspect the medication for particles or discoloration before use; if either is present, do not use the liquid. Clean the injection site with rubbing alcohol before each dose, and rotate injection sites to minimize skin injury. Avoid injecting into areas of skin that are sore, bruised, red, or hard. To reduce bruising, do not rub the injection site after administration. Use this medication consistently to achieve the best results. To help you remember, mark your calendar with the days you need to administer the medication. Common side effects include redness, itching, pain, or swelling at the injection site. Keep in mind that your doctor has prescribed this medication because they believe the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. In rare cases, adalimumab may cause severe, potentially fatal liver disease in individuals exposed to the hepatitis B virus. Your doctor may order blood tests and monitor you for symptoms during treatment and for several months after your last dose. Serious allergic reactions to this medication are rare. However, this is not a comprehensive list of possible side effects. In the United States, contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for similar guidance. Before using adalimumab, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, any other adalimumab products, or any other substances. This product may contain inactive ingredients, such as natural rubber or latex, which can cause allergic reactions or other issues. Adalimumab can increase your susceptibility to infections or worsen existing infections. Avoid contact with individuals who have contagious infections, such as chickenpox, COVID-19, measles, or the flu. Inform your healthcare provider that you are using adalimumab before receiving any immunizations or vaccinations. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly necessary, as it may harm an unborn baby. Discuss the risks and benefits with your doctor. Adalimumab can also pass into breast milk. Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase your risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. This document does not include all possible drug interactions. If someone overdoses and exhibits severe symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. While using this medication, your doctor may recommend regular lab tests, such as complete blood counts and liver function tests, to monitor your health. Keep all medical and lab appointments. If you miss a dose, consult your doctor or pharmacist promptly for a new dosing schedule. Store this medication in the refrigerator and do not freeze it. Keep it in its original container to protect it from light. Some brands of this medication may also be stored at room temperature if necessary. Consult your pharmacist or the product packaging for specific storage instructions. Discard any unused portion of the medication. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly dispose of this product when it is expired or no longer needed. In a medical emergency, your condition may cause complications. Always ensure your healthcare providers are aware of your medical history and current treatments. This information was last revised in September 2024. For complete and personalized medical advice, consult your healthcare professional.
